support: Where should Vantara's support team focus?
Reporting has 58 of 269 incidents, including 22 tagged P1. Invoicing follows with 53 incidents and 21 P1 cases. That makes both useful review priorities.
Is this a repeat problem, or just old tickets?
The 22 reporting P1 cases span June 2024 to April 2026. Two subjects describe dashboard slowness over a long date range. Matching subjects are a lead, not proof of one recurring defect.
Show me a source, and explain the calculation.
TKT-22426 records a dashboard/API discrepancy. It is tagged P1 and solved. Reporting's incident share is 58 ÷ 269 = 21.6%. Recorded status does not establish resolution quality.
What should the owner do next, and how would we know it worked?

Review the reporting and Invoicing cases together. Confirm symptoms and closure quality, then link product issues where the evidence supports it. Measure recurrence and reopened cases after an approved fix.
contracts: Compare the Growth and Enterprise agreements. What matters?
Enterprise targets 99.95% uptime, a 10-minute P0 response, and a 2-hour resolution. Growth targets 99.5%, 30 minutes, and 8 hours. Nine matched terms reveal service, process, and remedy differences.
Which differences would affect the way we operate?

Enterprise requires seven days' maintenance notice versus two. Billing disputes have 7 versus 15 business days. API availability and latency targets also tighten. Each difference belongs with its operational owner.
Show the source behind the response target. What about credits?
Section 3.2 confirms the 10 versus 30-minute response target. Credit caps are 100% versus 25%, but the qualifying conditions differ. Compare the conditions with the cap, not the percentages alone.
Turn that into a practical review plan.

Legal and the service owner should verify the signed agreement and amendments, map obligations to operating controls, and check any remedy against the qualifying conditions. Escalate confirmed mismatches for review.
Proposed commercial review / no breach established
regions: East leads on contract value. Should West copy its approach?
East records $217.590M in won annual contract value; West records $173.875M. The $43.715M lead is real in this sample. It does not, by itself, show that East's approach is better.
East and West / all recorded opportunities
Is the gap mostly deal volume or deal size?
East has 365 more won deals. At West's average value, those deals explain $40.735M of the gap. The remaining $2.980M comes from average deal value. This is a descriptive breakdown.
Does the account mix change the picture? Show the source.
East has 14 indexed accounts; West has 11. West's won value per indexed account is 1.7% higher. Customer and prospect mixes differ, so this is not a fair productivity comparison.
What would justify a change in West?
Ask sales operations for matched, dated groups. Test opportunity supply and win conversion separately. Propose a coverage pilot only for a verified supply gap, with a baseline and review criteria.
issues: Which high-priority product issues should we review first?
Of 1,360 issues tagged high or highest, 20 are marked in progress. Checkout, Billing, and Invoicing have six each; Developer APIs has two. Start with that scoped review set.
Are those 20 all bugs? Does the biggest backlog mean biggest risk?
The active set includes 4 bugs, 9 tasks, and 7 stories. Revenue Analytics has 248 historical high-priority records but none in progress. Backlog size alone does not establish business risk.
Open one of the Checkout issues. How did you choose it?
ISS-001 describes a blank Hosted Checkout on Safari iOS. It is tagged high and in progress, recorded January 10, 2025. It is one of six matching Checkout records, not a proven top-impact issue.
What should the product owner do with this?

Confirm current status, affected customers, and linked incidents. Rank the verified impact alongside engineering effort. After an approved fix, review linked incidents and closure quality against the baseline.
